blocks.title: Abstract
blocks.content:
Deep Research systems have revolutionized how LLMs solve com-
plex questions through iterative reasoning and evidence gathering.
However, current systems remain fundamentally constrained to
textual web data, overlooking the vast knowledge embedded in mul-
timodal documents: scientific papers, technical reports, and finan-
cial documents where critical information exists in figures, tables,
charts, and equations. Processing such documents demands sophis-
ticated parsing to preserve visual semantics, intelligent chunking to
maintain structural coherence, and adaptive retrieval across modal-
itie

summary.text: Abstract of Doc-Researcher. Deep Research systems are limited to textual web data, while scientific papers, technical reports and financial documents keep critical information in figures, tables, charts and equations. Doc-Researcher combines (i) deep multimodal parsing that keeps layout and visual semantics and builds representations from chunk to document level, (ii) retrieval that supports text-only, vision-only and hybrid paradigms with dynamic granularity selection, and (iii) iterative multi-agent workflows that decompose queries and accumulate evidence. The authors also introduce M4DocBench, a benchmark of 158 expert-annotated questions with complete evidence chains over 304 documents, for multi-modal, multi-hop, multi-document and multi-turn deep research. They report 50.6% accuracy, 3.4× the best baseline. The block ends with the CCS concepts, keywords and the ACM copyright notice.

blocks.title: Introduction
blocks.content:
Recently, agentic retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems
have significantly transformed the way LLMs retrieve, organize,
and present information [30, 43]. Agentic RAG enhances tradi-
tional RAG paradigm by enabling systems to plan retrieval strate-
gies, invoke external tools, adaptively refine queries, and validate
context [18]. These capabilities underpin recent Deep Research
systems [13], which support complex reasoning [14, 17–19] and
research workflows [9, 20]. However, current deep research sys-
tems [37] remain constrained by their exclusive focus on textual
web data. This limitat

summary.text: Introduction. Agentic RAG lets systems plan retrieval, call tools, refine queries and validate context, and it underpins current Deep Research systems; but these work only on textual web data and cannot use a person's own local documents. Multimodal agentic RAG systems such as MDocAgent and M3DocRAG have three limitations, the authors argue: (1) shallow parsing, either OCR text or raw page screenshots, which loses the semantics of charts, tables, figures, equations and layout; (2) retrieval over OCR chunks or whole pages only, with no way to pick a granularity (full text, summary, page or chunk) to suit the query; and (3) single-round visual QA instead of iterative, multi-step research. They add that no evaluation framework tests multimodal document understanding in realistic research settings. The block ends mid-sentence at a page break.

blocks.title: Related Work
blocks.content:
Our work builds upon three research directions that collectively
define the landscape of multimodal document understanding.
Document Parsing Strategies. Document parsing approaches
fall into three categories, each with distinct tradeoffs. Shallow
parsing relies on OCR to extract text while discarding spatial and
visual information [31]. Deep parsing systems like MinerU [39]
preserve layout structure through bounding boxes, transcribe equa-
tions to LaTeX [38], and convert tables to structured formats [42].
Recent VLM-based parsers [21, 27] further enhance extraction
quality. Parsing-free appro

summary.text: Related work, first two of three directions. Document parsing comes in three kinds: shallow parsing (OCR text only, losing spatial and visual information), deep parsing such as MinerU (layout boxes, equations to LaTeX, tables to structured formats, recently VLM-based), and parsing-free approaches that treat pages as screenshots, which avoids parsing cost but loses fine-grained localisation and copes poorly with dense text. The authors say their framework combines the strengths of the deep and parsing-free kinds. Visual document understanding benchmarks have moved from single pages to multi-page and long documents, but none test multi-document synthesis, multi-turn interaction or evidence-chain annotation, which motivates M4DocBench. The rest of the block is the text layer of Figure 2 (the architecture diagram): labels for the offline parsing and indexing stage and the online research stage.

blocks.content:
Figure 2: Doc-Researcher Architecture: (a) multimodal deep parsing and indexing, and (b) multimodal deep research.
Document RAG Systems. Due to limited context windows,
DocRAG systems have merged that decompose understanding
into retrieval and reasoning stages. Current systems [3, 6, 12]
employ various strategies: M3DocRAG uses vision-only page re-
trieval, MDocAgent combines text chunks with screenshots, and
VDocRAG [32] incorporates figure extraction. However, all perform
single-round retrieval with fixed granularities, lacking the iterative
refinement and adaptive strategies essential for c

summary.text: Despite its heading, this block holds the caption of Figure 2 (the Doc-Researcher architecture: (a) multimodal deep parsing and indexing, (b) multimodal deep research) and the third related-work direction, document RAG. M3DocRAG uses vision-only page retrieval, MDocAgent combines text chunks with screenshots, and VDocRAG adds figure extraction, but all do single-round retrieval at a fixed granularity. The authors present Doc-Researcher as the first deep-research framework for multimodal documents, with dynamic granularity selection and progressive evidence synthesis.

blocks.title: Method: Doc-Researcher
blocks.content:
Doc-Researcher (in Figure 2) consists of two main modules: deep
parsing and deep research. The deep parsing pipeline transforms
multimodal documents into structured, multi-granular, and search-
able units while preserving multimodal semantics. The deep re-
search adopts a multi-agent collaborative framework to solve com-
plex questions with iterative search and refinement.
3.1

summary.text: Opening of the method section. Doc-Researcher (Figure 2) has two modules: deep parsing, which turns multimodal documents into structured, multi-granular, searchable units while keeping their multimodal semantics, and deep research, a multi-agent framework that answers complex questions by iterative search and refinement.

blocks.title: Deep Multimodal Document Parsing
blocks.content:
Multi-modal Doc Parsing. Given a collection of multimodal doc-
uments D, each document 𝑑𝑖∈D undergoes layout-aware parsing
via MinerU [39] to extract structural elements 𝐸𝑖= {𝑒𝑖,𝑗,𝑘}, where
indices denote document 𝑖, page 𝑗, and reading sequence 𝑘. Each el-
ement is pair with its layout type (text, table, figure, equation), and
bounding box coordinates (Figure 5a). For computational efficiency,
we perform one-time textual conversion of visual elements. Tables
and figures are processed through Qwen2.5-VL [1] to generate both
coarse-grained summaries for contextual understanding and f

summary.text: Section 3.1, deep multimodal document parsing. Each document is parsed with MinerU into layout elements indexed by document, page and reading order, each with a type (text, table, figure, equation) and a bounding box. Tables and figures are described once by Qwen2.5-VL, as both a coarse summary and a fine-grained description; equations are converted to LaTeX with UniMERNet. This one-time conversion avoids processing multimodal tokens repeatedly. Layout-aware chunking then merges text elements within section boundaries up to a maximum length, keeping page IDs and boxes for citation. Four granularities are built: chunk, page (merged elements or the raw screenshot), full text, and an LLM-written document summary.

blocks.title: Multimodal Retrieval Architecture
blocks.content:
Vision-only Retrieval. Vision-only retrieval operates at page gran-
ularity using raw screenshots as encoded passages. This approach
eliminates parsing overhead, offering high efficiency without OCR
or layout analysis. However, it faces challenges in representing
complex interleaved text-vision content through dense vectors. For
high-resolution pages, multi-vector vision retrievers can produce
thousands of vectors, as each small image patch (typically 16x16 or
14x14 pixels) correspond to a vector. Additionally, vision retrievers
rely on parameter-heavy VLMs (often >3B parameters) with deeper
a

summary.text: Section 3.2, the three retrieval paradigms. Vision-only retrieval encodes raw page screenshots: no parsing cost, but dense vectors represent interleaved text and images poorly, multi-vector retrievers produce thousands of vectors per page (one per 14×14 or 16×16 patch), and the models are large (often over 3B parameters). Text-only retrieval encodes OCR text, chunks and VLM descriptions of visual elements at page or chunk level with small models (often under 1B), at the cost of preprocessing and some lost visual semantics. Hybrid retrieval encodes visual chunks and screenshots directly alongside text, avoiding conversion loss but costing more at inference. Between the paragraphs is the text layer of Table 1, which compares M4DocBench with ten document RAG/VQA datasets on multi-hop, multimodal, multi-document and multi-turn support, question count, annotation type, domains, languages and retrieval annotation; M4DocBench is the only one with all four properties, with 158 questions, 3.8 documents, 7.0 pages and 14.8 layout elements of evidence per question.
Heading-only block: it holds just the number "4.1" of the first subsection of the M4DocBench section, whose text is in the next block.

blocks.title: Motivation of M4DocBench
blocks.content:
Existing evaluation benchmarks fail to capture the complexity of
multimodal document deep research. A comprehensive evaluation
must assess four critical dimensions: (1) Multi-hop reasoning:
Complex questions requiring sophisticated reasoning chains across
evidence. (2) Multi-modal integration: Questions demanding
information from at least two modalities (text, tables, images). (3)
Multi-document synthesis: Questions relying evidence from mul-
tiple documents, where each document provides unique, essential
information. Distractor documents with topically related content
increase retrieval diffi

summary.text: Section 4.1, why M4DocBench. A deep-research benchmark must test four things: multi-hop reasoning, multimodal integration (at least two modalities per question), multi-document synthesis (each document contributing essential information, with topically similar distractors), and multi-turn dialogue. Table 1 shows that most existing DocVQA/RAG datasets have multi-hop and multimodal evidence but only one has genuine multi-document reasoning; evidence averages under two pages per question; only two give layout-level evidence; and none is multi-turn. A footnote says that adding noise documents to single-document questions does not make a true multi-document setting. M4DocBench is presented as filling these gaps with expert-annotated QA pairs and complete evidence chains.

blocks.title: Domain and Document Collection
blocks.content:
We select four distinct domains (research, insurance, education, and
finance) based on three criteria: (1) Multimodal richness: Each
domain features essential visual elements (tables, charts, figures) in-
tegrated with text; (2) Reasoning complexity: Questions require
diverse capabilities from technical comprehension to numerical
analysis; (3) Practical relevance: These represent real-world sce-
narios where professionals routinely conduct document research.
We collect documents from authoritative sources to ensure quality
and representativeness:
• Research: We collect 166 computer science pap

summary.text: Section 4.2, domains and documents. Four domains were chosen for multimodal richness, reasoning complexity and practical relevance: research (166 computer-science papers from arXiv and top conferences, averaging 26.7 pages), insurance (43 brochures and policy documents, 11.0 pages), education (56 university programme materials, 7.5 pages) and finance (38 market research reports on A-shares, Hong Kong and NASDAQ, 22.2 pages).

blocks.title: Annotation Process
blocks.content:
Our annotation process employs PhD/Master-level researchers with
extensive research experience to ensure benchmark quality. Beyond
basic question-answer pairs, we annotate six critical dimensions
that enable comprehensive evaluation of deep research systems:
• Hard Negative Documents: We carefully curate documents
that share topical similarity with target questions while lacking
essential information. This tests systems’ ability to distinguish
truly relevant sources from plausible distractors—a critical capa-
bility for effective document filtering in large collections.
• Retrieval Granularity

summary.text: Section 4.3, annotation. PhD- and Master's-level researchers annotated, beyond question-answer pairs, six dimensions: hard-negative documents that are topically similar but lack the needed information; the best retrieval granularity for each query (full text, summary, page or chunk); relevant pages and bounding boxes, following MMDocIR; ground-truth sub-query decompositions; answer-verification checklists for long answers, used for LLM-based judging; and bilingual English and Chinese questions and documents. Figure 1 and Figure 4 show annotation examples.

blocks.title: Evaluation Metrics and Benchmarks
blocks.content:
Multimodal Retrieval Evaluation. We evaluate retrieval per-
formance at three granularities aligned with our retrieval frame-
work (§3.2): document, page, and layout. For each granularity, we
compute recall@k by comparing retrieved passages2 against gold
annotations. Document and page recall are computed using exact ID
matching. For chunk-level evaluation, following Dong et al. [5], we
calculate recall based on bounding box overlap between retrieved
and gold-standard layouts. Note that parsing-free methods cannot
be evaluated at chunk granularity.
Deep Research Evaluation. We evaluate the comp

summary.text: Section 5.1, metrics and benchmarks. Retrieval is scored as recall@k at document, page and layout level: document and page by exact ID match, layout by bounding-box overlap following MMDocIR (parsing-free methods cannot be scored at layout level). The full deep-research workflow is scored on document selection (precision, recall and F1 of the Planner's chosen documents), agentic retrieval (the same recall metrics over the passages accumulated after the search-refine loops), and answer accuracy, judged by an LLM against the annotated checklist; an answer counts as correct only when every checklist item is present. The two benchmarks are M4DocBench and MMDocIR. Most of the block is the text layer of Table 2, recall@10 of text, vision and hybrid retrievers (BM25, E5, BGE-M3, Qwen3-embedding, DSE, ColPali, ColQwen, Jina-embedding-v4 and combinations) on both benchmarks; the block is cut off inside the table.

blocks.title: System Setting and Baselines
blocks.content:
Retrieval System. We evaluate 10 retrievers to implement our
multimodal retrieval architecture (§3.2): 5 Text retrievers: BM25
[28], E5 [40], BGE-M3 [2], Qwen3-embedding-0.6B [45], and Qwen3-
reranker-0.6B [45]. 5 Vision retrievers: DSE [22], ColPali [10],
ColQwen [10], and Jina-embedding-v4 [11] (multi-vector and dense
variants). We configure these retrievers in three paradigms: (1)
Text-only: Text retrievers encode both textual and visual chunks,
with visual elements represented through VLM descriptions. (2)
Vision-only: Vision retrievers directly retrieve page screenshots
without parsing. (

summary.text: Section 5.2, setup and baselines. Ten retrievers are tested in three configurations: five text retrievers (BM25, E5, BGE-M3, Qwen3-embedding-0.6B, Qwen3-reranker-0.6B) and vision retrievers (DSE, ColPali, ColQwen, and multi-vector and dense Jina-embedding-v4), used text-only (visual elements via VLM descriptions), vision-only (page screenshots, no parsing) or hybrid. Sub-query results are reranked with Qwen3-reranker for text and accumulated equally per sub-query for vision and hybrid. Doc-Researcher runs with Qwen3-32B, Qwen3-235B or DeepSeek-R1 as backbone at three parsing levels: parsing-free (screenshots, plus InternVL3.5-38B to read them), shallow (fixed-length OCR chunks) and deep (layout-aware chunks with VLM transcriptions). Baselines are direct answering with no documents, long context (documents truncated at 96k tokens), and existing document RAG systems. The rest of the block is the text layer of Table 3, accuracy by language and domain, document-selection scores and retrieval recall per configuration; it is cut off inside the table.

blocks.content:
Table 2 presents retrieval performance across different paradigms
on M4DocBench and MMDocIR, evaluating both original questions
and decomposed sub-queries. Fine-grained results are in Figure 7.
Retrieval Paradigm Comparison. Text-only retrieval shows
hierarchical performance: sparse retrieval (BM25) performs worst,
while dense retrievers (BGE-M3, Qwen3-Embedding) achieve sub-
stantial improvements. Vision-only retrieval, Jina-embedding-v4,
even its dense variant, outperform other multi-vector models. Note
that vision-only retrieval excels text-only method on MMDocIR’s
visual-centric tasks but

summary.text: Section 5.3, retrieval results (Table 2, details in Figure 7). Among text retrievers BM25 is weakest and dense retrievers (BGE-M3, Qwen3-Embedding) much better. Among vision retrievers Jina-embedding-v4, even dense, beats the other multi-vector models. Vision-only beats text-only on MMDocIR's visual tasks but not on M4DocBench's multi-document questions. Hybrid retrieval beats either single modality throughout: Qwen3-Embedding with Jina-embedding-v4 improves page recall by 8–12% over either alone. Sub-query decomposition helps every paradigm, for example Qwen3-Embedding page recall at k=15 from 42.1% to 49.9%. Recall falls with granularity: over 70% at document level for hybrid methods, 30–40 points lower at page and layout level.

blocks.title: Main Results: Multimodal Deep Research
blocks.content:
Table 3 validates our core contributions via systematic comparisons.
Deep Research can largely improve multimodal understand-
ing. Direct answering achieves only 5-10%; long-context processing
ranges within 9-31% despite document content of 96k tokens is
given. Results show that neither parametric knowledge nor brute-
force context extension can handle research-level complexity. In
comparison, Doc-Researcher with multi-agent framework (with
strategic planning, iterative search-refine loops, and progressive
evidence accumulation) achieves score of 50.6%. The 20-40% gap
over long-context proves

summary.text: Section 5.4, main results (Table 3). Direct answering scores 5–10% and long context 9–31%, while Doc-Researcher reaches 50.6%, which the authors take to show that research-level questions need a multi-agent workflow, not more context. Shallow parsing gives 34–39%, below parsing-free screenshots at 36–43%; deep parsing with hybrid retrieval gives 42–50%, about 10 points better. Baseline document RAG systems do poorly because they retrieve once with a fixed strategy: MDocAgent 15.8%, M3DocRAG 7.0%, ColQwen-gen 5.7%; Doc-Researcher's 50.6% is 3.4× MDocAgent. The block also holds the text layer and caption of Figure 3, accuracy, accumulated chunks and document, page and layout recall over search turns 1–5 for the three backbones, with accuracy gains of +7.2%, +9.7% and +11.1%.

blocks.title: Ablation Study
blocks.content:
We ablate components of Doc-Researcher, and validate different
architectural design as follows:
Hybrid Retrieval Necessity. Within our deep parsing frame-
work, hybrid retrieval (42.4-50.6%) outperforms text-only (39.2-
45.6%) by 3-5%. This shows that even with high-quality textual
transcriptions in both coarse and fine-grained level, some visual se-
mantics is lost. In comparison, visual encoders that directly encode
using chunk image, can capture irreplaceable semantics. This vali-
dates our hybrid retrieval design over single-modality approaches.
Adaptive Planning Impact. Removing the Plann

summary.text: Section 5.5, ablations. Within deep parsing, hybrid retrieval (42.4–50.6%) beats text-only (39.2–45.6%) by 3–5 points, so some visual meaning is lost even with good transcriptions. Removing the Planner costs 6–8 points, since the system then retrieves chunks uniformly from the noisy document set without filtering documents or choosing granularity. Over search turns (Figure 3), document recall rises from 62–65% at turn 1 to 75–82% at turn 3 and levels off near 82–83% by turn 5; accuracy rises from turn 1 to turn 5 by 7.2 points for Qwen3-32B, 9.7 for Qwen3-235B and 11.1 for DeepSeek-R1, mostly in turns 1–3, while accumulated chunks grow from 7–10 to 14–17. Stronger models use fewer chunks (DeepSeek-R1 14.1 against Qwen3-32B 17.2 at turn 5). Layout recall goes from 24–26% to 40–45%. The authors suggest three iterations as a good balance of quality and cost.

summary.text: Section 5.6, efficiency (Table 4, whose text layer is in this block), on M4DocBench's 304 documents (6,177 pages, 4,146 figures, 2,739 tables) and 158 questions. Deep parsing takes about 2.5 hours up front, against 9–39 minutes for parsing-free indexing, mostly for MinerU layout analysis and VLM transcription. But at research time parsing-free methods spend about 20 hours, 80% of inference, reading screenshots, while deep parsing finishes the same questions in about 4 hours, a 5× speedup. Multi-vector embeddings take 10–20× the storage and about 4× the indexing time of dense ones, and current vector databases do not support their late-interaction search. For deep parsing, research time splits into about 2 hours planning, 4 hours of search-refine loops and 2 hours answering.

blocks.title: Conclusion
blocks.content:
We introduced Doc-Researcher, addressing the critical limitation
that existing deep research systems cannot process multimodal doc-
uments. Our work identifies and resolves three fundamental gaps
in current systems. First, we developed a deep multimodal parsing
framework that preserves layout structure and modality-specific
characteristics, achieving 11.4% improvement over simplistic OCR
approaches. Second, we designed a systematic retrieval architec-
ture supporting multiple paradigms (text/vision/hybrid) and gran-
ularities (chunk/page/full/summary). Third, we implement itera-
tive multi-age

summary.text: Conclusion. The authors restate their three contributions: deep multimodal parsing that keeps layout and modality-specific features (11.4% better than simple OCR), a retrieval architecture over text, vision and hybrid paradigms and chunk, page, full and summary granularities, and iterative multi-agent workflows with planning and search-refine loops (3.4× the best baseline); plus M4DocBench, 158 expert-annotated questions over 4 domains. Future work: compact multimodal embeddings, better cross-modal reasoning, and active learning that adapts retrieval to user interaction.

summary.text: Reference list of the paper, pages 9–13: 46 numbered entries, 36 of them from 2024 or 2025 and 31 on arXiv. They cover vision-language models and embeddings (Qwen2.5-VL, Qwen3, BGE-M3, E5, ColPali, Jina-embedding-v4, DSE), document parsing (MinerU, UniMERNet), document VQA and RAG benchmarks and systems (MMDocIR, ViDoRe, DocBench, M3DocRAG, MDocAgent), and agentic RAG and deep-research systems.

blocks.content: A page from a CVSource (投中信息) Chinese-language investment-research report headed "A轮交易占市场近半数 广东投资数量荣登榜首" (A-round deals are nearly half the market; Guangdong leads on deal count). A page from a CVSource (投中信息) Chinese-language investment-research report with the same heading "港交所主板账面退出回报最高", for May 2025. A red rectangle covers the opening paragraph and the exit-analysis table; the bar-and-line chart beneath runs 2024-05 to 2025-05. A narrow screenshot of an NUS page headed "Master of Computing (Computer Science Specialisation) (Coursework)", with an orange "Explore Our Programmes" banner at the top, a dark blue technology hero image in the middle, two orange call-to-action buttons ("More Info", "Apply Now"), and Faculty and description text beneath.

A brochure page for the NUS MTech in Artificial Intelligence Systems. The upper half covers English Language Proficiency (TOEFL and IELTS thresholds in a small table) and the GRE/NUS-ISS entrance test, with a "How to Apply" panel. The lower half holds the Programme Schedule as two coloured grids -- full-time over two semesters, part-time over four -- followed by notes on the Practice Module and the Stackable Graduate Certificate Programme.

A full one-page brochure for the NUS Master of Science in Quantitative Finance, in the university's blue and orange. Panels cover Overview, Faculty, Career Opportunities, Programme Structure and Candidature, Admission Requirements, How to Apply and two student testimonials. A red rectangle marks the candidature paragraph -- a 40-unit programme of five core and five elective courses, completable in 1 to 2 years full-time or 2 to 4 part-time.

A web page headed "Master of Technology in Enterprise Business Analytics" from NUS-ISS. A red rectangle encloses the Overview table -- next intake, duration, application timeline, entrance test and GRE arrangements -- above descriptive paragraphs and a list of what graduates will be able to do.

A page rendered from a markdown file, its header reading "27.nus-ba.md" and "2025-07-26", about the NUS Master of Science in Business Analytics. A red rectangle encloses the Commitment and Candidature table -- full time 14 months average and 24 maximum, part time 24 and 48 -- with target audience and admission criteria beneath.

A web page section for the NUS MSc in Digital Financial Technology. A red rectangle encloses the Commitment and Candidature table -- full time 1.5 years average and 3 years maximum, part time 2.5 and 3 -- with Scholarships above and Target Audience and General Admission Criteria (GMAT 650/800, TOEFL 90/120, IELTS 6.0/9) beneath.

A page from a CVSource (投中信息) Chinese-language investment-research report headed "全球：中企IPO首日破发率43.75%" (global: 43.75% of Chinese-company IPOs broke issue on day one). Two ranked tables give the top five first-day risers and fallers for April 2024, and a horizontal bar chart below shows the distribution of first-day moves across bands from -60%,-30% up to 240%,270%.

Page 3 of the paper "Actions Speak Louder than Words: Trillion-Parameter Sequential Transducers for Generative Recommendations", reproduced as it stands. It carries Figure 2 (a comparison of features and training procedures for DLRMs against Generative Recommenders), two columns of body text under headings 2.2 and 2.3, and Table 1. It is the parser's input, shown before any layout analysis.

The same page of "Actions Speak Louder than Words", overlaid with the parser's layout analysis. Fifteen regions are tinted and numbered 1 to 15 -- green for the figure, blue for the caption and the section headings, pink for body-text paragraphs, yellow for the table -- so that each detected element and its reading order can be read off directly.
